lead: The greatest common divisor (gcd) of two integers a and b is the largest positive integer that divides both. Euclid's algorithm finds it by repeated division: each remainder becomes the new divisor, and the last nonzero remainder is the gcd. The extended version also returns integers x and y with ax + by = gcd(a,b). That pair is how cryptography computes modular inverses, for example the private exponent in RSA and inverse elements inside finite-field arithmetic. Both algorithms are short, exact and fast: O(log min(a,b)) divisions.
prereq: You need: remainders and congruences from Chapter 2.1, especially the meaning of a mod n and the fact that a ≡ b (mod n) when n divides a−b.

blocks.text: The greatest common divisor of positive integers a and b is the largest positive integer d that divides both; write it gcd(a,b). For example gcd(252,105)=21. Euclid's algorithm uses one fact: the gcd does not change when the larger number is replaced by its remainder modulo the smaller number.

Start with r<sub>0</sub>=a, r<sub>1</sub>=b, a>b>0. Divide r<sub>0</sub> by r<sub>1</sub>: r<sub>0</sub>=q<sub>1</sub>r<sub>1</sub>+r<sub>2</sub>, where q<sub>1</sub>=⌊r<sub>0</sub>/r<sub>1</sub>⌋ is the quotient and 0 ≤ r<sub>2</sub> < r<sub>1</sub> is the remainder. Then gcd(r<sub>0</sub>,r<sub>1</sub>)=gcd(r<sub>1</sub>,r<sub>2</sub>). Replace (r<sub>0</sub>,r<sub>1</sub>) by (r<sub>1</sub>,r<sub>2</sub>) and repeat. The remainders decrease strictly, so some remainder becomes 0. The last nonzero remainder is gcd(a,b).

blocks.where: r0 and r1 are the current pair; q=⌊r0/r1⌋ is the quotient; r2 is the remainder. The gcd is unchanged by replacing (r0,r1) with (r1,r2).

items: While r1≠0, compute q=⌊r0/r1⌋ and r2=r0−q r1.

blocks.text: Why it works: any common divisor of r0 and r1 divides r0−q r1=r2, and any common divisor of r1 and r2 divides q r1+r2=r0. The two pairs have the same common divisors, so the same gcd. The loop takes O(log min(a,b)) divisions; each division works on numbers no larger than a.

The extended Euclidean algorithm returns g=gcd(a,b) and integers x,y with ax+by=g. This is Bézout's identity; x and y are Bézout coefficients and may be negative. For a=252,b=105 the result is 21=(−2)×252+5×105, so x=−2,y=5. Some syllabi call it extended GCD.

Keep two coefficient pairs. Set s<sub>0</sub>=1,s<sub>1</sub>=0 and t<sub>0</sub>=0,t<sub>1</sub>=1. At each division r<sub>0</sub>=q r<sub>1</sub>+r<sub>2</sub>, compute s<sub>2</sub>=s<sub>0</sub>−q s<sub>1</sub> and t<sub>2</sub>=t<sub>0</sub>−q t<sub>1</sub>. Then shift r<sub>0</sub>←r<sub>1</sub>, r<sub>1</sub>←r<sub>2</sub>; s<sub>0</sub>←s<sub>1</sub>, s<sub>1</sub>←s<sub>2</sub>; t<sub>0</sub>←t<sub>1</sub>, t<sub>1</sub>←t<sub>2</sub>. Stop when r<sub>2</sub>=0. Output g=r<sub>1</sub>, x=s<sub>1</sub>, y=t<sub>1</sub>.

The invariant r<sub>i</sub>=s<sub>i</sub>a+t<sub>i</sub>b holds at the start and survives every update. Back-substitution is the same calculation written upward from the last division. The table method avoids sign errors because each new coefficient uses one multiplication and one subtraction.

If gcd(a,n)=1, the integers a and n are coprime. Extended Euclid gives ax+ny=1. Modulo n this becomes ax≡1 (mod n), so x mod n is the inverse a<sup>−1</sup> mod n. RSA uses this: d=e<sup>−1</sup> mod φ(n) when gcd(e,φ(n))=1; see Unit 4, RSA cryptosystem.
If gcd(a,n)=g>1, no inverse exists. Every multiple of a modulo n is a multiple of g, so none can equal 1 modulo n. Cancelling a in a congruence is valid only when gcd(a,n)=1.
Running time: remainders shrink by at least half every two steps, so the loop has O(log min(a,b)) divisions. The extended version adds constant work per division, so it has the same bound.

figure.caption: Each division cuts the previous number into copies of the divisor plus a remainder: 42, then 21, then 0, so gcd(252, 105) = 21. The s and t columns in row 3 give the coefficients: 252 × (−2) + 105 × 5 = 21.

spec.aria: Three bars: 252 split into 105, 105 and 42; 105 split into 42, 42 and 21; 42 split into 21 and 21. Below, the extended Euclid table with row 3 (r = 21, s = −2, t = 5) highlighted and the check.

examples.question: Use the extended Euclidean algorithm on a=252 and b=105. Find g=gcd(252,105), and integers x,y with 252x+105y=g. Show every division and check the result.
steps: Divide: 42=2×21+0, so q=2 and r2=0. Then s2=1−2×(−2)=5 and t2=−2−2×5=−12. Remainder is 0, so stop.
Last nonzero remainder is r1=21, so g=21. Coefficients are x=s1=−2 and y=t1=5.
examples.answer: The gcd is 21, with x=−2 and y=5, so 21=(−2)×252+5×105.
examples.check:
def egcd(a, b):
    r0, r1 = a, b
    s0, s1 = 1, 0
    t0, t1 = 0, 1
    while r1 != 0:
        q = r0 // r1
        r0, r1 = r1, r0 - q * r1
        s0, s1 = s1, s0 - q * s1
        t0, t1 = t1, t0 - q * t1
    return r0, s0, t0

g, x, y = egcd(252, 105)
print(g)
print(x)
print(y)

traps: Losing signs when back-substituting; write r<sub>i</sub> = r<sub>i−2</sub> − q<sub>i−1</sub> r<sub>i−1</sub>, where q<sub>i−1</sub> = ⌊r<sub>i−2</sub>/r<sub>i−1</sub>⌋, and multiply out to check.
Calling x a modular inverse when gcd(a,n)>1; an inverse exists only for coprime a and n.
Swapping quotient and remainder; q=⌊a/b⌋, r=a−qb, and 0 ≤ r < b.
Stopping at the first zero remainder and returning the wrong coefficients; stop when r2=0, then output x=s1 and y=t1.

quiz.q: State what Euclid's algorithm returns for positive integers a>b.
quiz.a: The last nonzero remainder in the repeated-division process; this is gcd(a,b).

quiz.q: Why does replacing (r0,r1) by (r1,r2) keep the gcd unchanged?
quiz.a: Because r2=r0−q r1, the common divisors of r0 and r1 are exactly the common divisors of r1 and r2, so both pairs have the same gcd.

quiz.q: Run Euclid's algorithm on 48 and 18. Give all remainders and the gcd.
quiz.a: 48=2×18+12; 18=1×12+6; 12=2×6+0. The last nonzero remainder is 6, so gcd(48,18)=6.

quiz.q: Use the extended Euclidean algorithm on 35 and 12 to find x,y with 35x+12y=1.
A student finds gcd(252,105)=21 and then writes 252<sup>−1</sup> mod 105. Explain the error.
quiz.a: An inverse modulo 105 needs gcd(252,105)=1. Here the gcd is 21>1, so no inverse exists; 252≡42 (mod 105), and multiples of 42 cannot give 1 modulo 105.

quiz.q: What two extra integers does the extended Euclidean algorithm return besides the gcd?
quiz.a: Integers x and y such that ax+by=gcd(a,b).

quiz.q: When is x mod n the modular inverse of a modulo n?
quiz.a: When gcd(a,n)=1 and ax+ny=1. Reducing modulo n gives ax≡1 (mod n), so x mod n is the inverse.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cryptographic libraries use extended Euclid to compute RSA private exponents and inverses in elliptic-curve field arithmetic, often with constant-time variants that avoid secret-dependent divisions. Binary GCD (Stein's algorithm) replaces division by shifts and subtraction, which is friendlier on some processors. Lehmer's algorithm speeds up gcd on large multiword integers. Search next for 'binary extended gcd', 'modular inverse constant time', and 'Bézout coefficients cryptography'.
